questions.question: Which tense is used in 'I've just been running'?

options.A: present perfect continuous

questions.correct_answer_text: present perfect continuous

steps: 'I've just been running' uses have + been + -ing, i.e. the present perfect continuous.
solution.summary: I've been running = present perfect continuous.

questions.explanation: The extract uses the present perfect continuous to describe a recent activity.

questions.question: Which tense is used in 'I'll be doing a 5k run for charity in a few weeks'?

options.A: future continuous

questions.correct_answer_text: future continuous

steps: 'I'll be doing' uses will + be + -ing, i.e. the future continuous.

questions.explanation: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a future time.

questions.question: Which tense is used in 'Had you done much running before?'?

options.A: past perfect

questions.correct_answer_text: past perfect

steps: 'Had you done' uses had + past participle, i.e. the past perfect.

questions.explanation: The past perfect describes an action that happened before a past time.

questions.question: Which tense is used in 'I will have been running every day for two months'?

options.A: future perfect continuous

questions.correct_answer_text: future perfect continuous

steps: 'Will have been running' uses will + have + been + -ing, i.e. the future perfect continuous.
solution.summary: will have been running = future perfect continuous.

questions.explanation: This tense describes how long an action will have continued by a future time.

questions.question: We use the present perfect continuous to ...

options.A: focus on the activity itself or its continuity

questions.correct_answer_text: focus on the activity itself or its continuity

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The present perfect continuous focuses on the activity and how long it continues.
solution.summary: Present perfect continuous = focus on continuity.

questions.explanation: It emphasises the ongoing activity rather than the finished result.

questions.question: We use the present perfect simple to ...

options.A: focus on a finished action and its present result
options.B: focus on the duration of an activity

questions.correct_answer_text: focus on a finished action and its present result

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The present perfect simple focuses on a completed action that has a result now.
solution.summary: Present perfect simple = finished action with result.

questions.explanation: It shows a completed action connected to the present.

questions.question: Which tense describes an action that was in progress at a moment in the past?

options.A: past continuous

questions.correct_answer_text: past continuous

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The past continuous (was/were + -ing) describes an action in progress in the past.
solution.summary: Past continuous = in progress in the past.

questions.explanation: Example: 'I was running for the bus when I tripped.'

questions.question: We use the past perfect to describe ...

options.A: an action that happened before another past action

questions.correct_answer_text: an action that happened before another past action

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The past perfect (had + past participle) refers to the earlier of two past actions.

questions.explanation: Example: 'Before I trained, I had never run in a race.'

questions.question: Which tense describes an action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future?

options.A: future continuous

questions.correct_answer_text: future continuous

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The future continuous (will be + -ing) describes an action in progress at a future time.
solution.summary: Future continuous = in progress in the future.

questions.explanation: Example: 'This time next week I'll be doing a 5k run.'

questions.question: We use the future perfect to describe ...

options.A: an action that will be finished by a certain time in the future
options.C: a completed action in the past

questions.correct_answer_text: an action that will be finished by a certain time in the future

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action finished by a future time.
solution.summary: Future perfect = finished by a future time.

questions.explanation: Example: 'When I finish the marathon, I will have run 42 km.'

questions.question: We use the future perfect continuous to describe ...

options.A: how long something will have been going on by a future time

questions.correct_answer_text: how long something will have been going on by a future time

source.reference: Grammar Reference: Continuous and perfect tenses

steps: The future perfect continuous emphasises the duration of an action up to a future time.
solution.summary: Future perfect continuous = duration up to a future time.

questions.explanation: Example: 'Next week I will have been running every day for two months.'

questions.question: In 'I've been reading a book about habits', the speaker ...

options.A: is still reading the book

questions.correct_answer_text: is still reading the book

steps: The present perfect continuous shows the action is still in progress, so the speaker is still reading.

questions.explanation: The continuous form shows the activity has not finished.

questions.question: In 'I've read a book about habits', the speaker ...

options.A: has finished the book

questions.correct_answer_text: has finished the book

steps: The present perfect simple describes a finished action.

questions.explanation: The simple form focuses on the completed result.

questions.question: In 'I will be working', the speaker ...

options.A: will be in the middle of work

questions.correct_answer_text: will be in the middle of work

steps: The future continuous shows the person will be in the middle of working.
solution.summary: I will be working = in the middle of work.

questions.explanation: The continuous form describes an action in progress at a future time.

questions.question: In 'I will have been working', the speaker ...

options.A: will have finished work
options.B: will be in the middle of work

questions.correct_answer_text: will have finished work

steps: The future perfect shows the work will be finished by that future time.
solution.summary: I will have been working = finished.

questions.explanation: The perfect form focuses on completion.

questions.question: In 'I had been eating all day', the meaning is that the person ...

options.A: was eating continuously or very often

questions.correct_answer_text: was eating continuously or very often

steps: 'Had been eating' is the past perfect continuous, which shows continuous or repeated eating.
solution.summary: I had been eating all day = eating continuously.

questions.explanation: The continuous form emphasises the repeated or continuous activity.

questions.question: In 'I had eaten that day', the meaning is that the person ...

options.A: ate at some point that day

questions.correct_answer_text: ate at some point that day

steps: 'Had eaten' is the past perfect simple, which describes one finished action.

questions.explanation: The simple form describes a single completed action.

questions.question: In 'I've come up with a great idea', the speaker ...

options.A: has the idea now

questions.correct_answer_text: has the idea now

steps: The present perfect shows the idea exists now as a result of a past action.
solution.summary: I've come up with = I have the idea now.

questions.explanation: The present perfect connects the past action to the present.

questions.question: In 'I had a great idea', the speaker ...

options.A: came up with an idea at some point in the past

questions.correct_answer_text: came up with an idea at some point in the past

steps: 'I had' is the past simple, describing an action at a past time.
solution.summary: I had a great idea = idea in the past.

questions.explanation: The past simple refers to a finished time in the past.

questions.question: 'I'm playing a lot of football' means ...

options.A: I've been doing it recently or temporarily
options.D: I did it in the past

questions.correct_answer_text: I've been doing it recently or temporarily

steps: The present continuous describes a temporary or recent activity.

questions.explanation: The continuous form shows it is happening around now.

questions.question: 'I play a lot of football' means ...

options.A: this is something I always do

questions.correct_answer_text: this is something I always do

steps: The present simple describes a permanent or regular activity.
solution.summary: I play = something I always do.

questions.explanation: The simple form shows a regular, permanent habit.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the past perfect continuous correctly?

options.A: I had been waiting for two hours when the bus finally arrived.
options.B: I had been waiting for two hours when the bus will arrive.
options.C: I have been waiting for two hours when the bus arrived.
options.D: I was waiting for two hours when the bus had arrived.

questions.correct_answer_text: I had been waiting for two hours when the bus finally arrived.

steps: The past perfect continuous (had been + -ing) describes an action continuing up to a past moment.

questions.explanation: The bus arrived (past simple) while the waiting was in progress.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the future perfect correctly?

options.A: By next year, I will have graduated from university.
options.B: By next year, I will have been graduating from university.
options.C: By next year, I am graduating from university.
options.D: By next year, I had graduated from university.

questions.correct_answer_text: By next year, I will have graduated from university.

steps: The future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action completed before a future time.

questions.explanation: The action (graduating) will be finished by next year.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'She ______ (work) here since 2019.'

options.A: has been working

questions.correct_answer_text: has been working

steps: 'Since 2019' indicates a period continuing to the present, so use the present perfect continuous.

questions.explanation: The action started in the past and continues now.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'They ______ (already/eat) by the time I arrived.'

options.A: had already eaten

questions.correct_answer_text: had already eaten

steps: The arrival is in the past, and the eating happened before it, so use the past perfect.

questions.explanation: The past perfect shows the earlier action.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'This time tomorrow, I ______ (lie) on the beach.'

options.A: will be lying

questions.correct_answer_text: will be lying

steps: 'This time tomorrow' points to an action in progress at a future time, so use the future continuous.

questions.explanation: The future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'By the time you get here, I ______ (finish) the report.'

options.A: will have finished

questions.correct_answer_text: will have finished

steps: 'By the time you get here' sets a future deadline, so use the future perfect.

questions.explanation: The action will be completed before the other future action.

questions.question: Which sentence shows the difference between 'I've been reading' and 'I've read'?

options.A: 'I've been reading' means I'm still reading; 'I've read' means I've finished.
options.B: 'I've been reading' means I finished; 'I've read' means I'm still reading.
options.D: 'I've been reading' is past; 'I've read' is future.

questions.correct_answer_text: 'I've been reading' means I'm still reading; 'I've read' means I've finished.

source.reference: Exercise 6: Present perfect simple vs continuous

steps: The continuous form emphasises the activity is ongoing; the simple form emphasises completion.

questions.explanation: This is the key difference between the two forms.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the past continuous?

options.A: I was studying when the power went out.
options.B: I had been studying when the power went out.
options.C: I have been studying when the power went out.
options.D: I studied when the power went out.

questions.correct_answer_text: I was studying when the power went out.

steps: The past continuous (was/were + -ing) describes an action in progress when another action interrupted.

questions.explanation: The studying was in progress when the power cut happened.

questions.question: Complete: 'I ______ (know) her since we were children.'

options.A: have known

questions.correct_answer_text: have known

steps: 'Since we were children' indicates a period from the past continuing to now, so use present perfect simple.

questions.explanation: The knowing started in the past and continues now.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the future perfect continuous correctly?

options.A: In June, I will have been working here for ten years.
options.B: In June, I will have worked here for ten years.
options.C: In June, I am working here for ten years.
options.D: In June, I had been working here for ten years.

questions.correct_answer_text: In June, I will have been working here for ten years.

steps: The future perfect continuous (will have been + -ing) emphasises the duration of an action up to a future time.

questions.explanation: It emphasises the length of service, not just the completion.

questions.question: Which is the correct transformation: 'People say she is kind' → Passive?

options.A: She is said to be kind.

questions.correct_answer_text: She is said to be kind.

steps: The structure is: subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive.
solution.summary: She is said to be kind.

questions.explanation: This passive structure reports what people say about someone.

questions.question: Which is correct: 'It is believed that he ______ (leave) yesterday'?

options.A: left

questions.correct_answer_text: left

steps: The reported action happened yesterday, so use the past simple in the that-clause.

questions.explanation: The past simple matches the time reference 'yesterday'.

questions.question: Which sentence is correct?

options.A: I had been cooking for an hour when the guests arrived.
options.B: I have been cooking for an hour when the guests arrived.
options.C: I was cooking for an hour when the guests arrived.
options.D: I cooked for an hour when the guests arrived.

questions.correct_answer_text: I had been cooking for an hour when the guests arrived.

steps: The cooking started before the arrival and was still in progress, so use the past perfect continuous.

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous shows the duration before a past event.

questions.question: Complete: 'She ______ (just/finish) her homework. Do you want to play?'

options.A: has just finished

questions.correct_answer_text: has just finished

steps: 'Just' with a recent action connected to the present uses the present perfect.

questions.explanation: The result (she can play now) is relevant to the present.

questions.question: Choose: 'By 2030, scientists ______ (probably/find) a cure for the disease.'

options.A: will probably have found

questions.correct_answer_text: will probably have found

steps: 'By 2030' sets a future deadline, so use the future perfect.

questions.explanation: The finding will be completed before 2030.

questions.question: Which sentence shows a temporary activity around now?

options.A: I'm reading a really interesting book at the moment.
options.B: I read a really interesting book every summer.
options.C: I have read a really interesting book.
options.D: I was reading a really interesting book last week.

questions.correct_answer_text: I'm reading a really interesting book at the moment.

steps: The present continuous with 'at the moment' describes a temporary activity happening now.

questions.explanation: The present simple ('I read') would describe a permanent habit.

questions.question: Which sentence describes a past action with a present result?

options.A: I've lost my keys, so I can't get in.
options.C: I was losing my keys when I ran.
options.D: I had lost my keys before I got home.

questions.correct_answer_text: I've lost my keys, so I can't get in.

source.reference: Exercise 6: Present perfect vs past simple

steps: The present perfect connects a past action (losing keys) to a present result (can't get in).

questions.explanation: The past simple ('I lost') would just state when it happened.

questions.question: Complete: 'We ______ (live) in this house since 2015.'

options.A: have lived

questions.correct_answer_text: have lived

steps: 'Since 2015' means from a point in the past until now, so use the present perfect.

questions.explanation: The action started in the past and continues to the present.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'When I ______ (get) to the party, everyone had already left.'

options.A: got

questions.correct_answer_text: got

steps: The past perfect 'had already left' needs a later past action (got) to relate to.

questions.explanation: The getting is the later past action; the leaving happened before it.
